name: Spirit Protocol (2025-26)
why: Announced 'social institution for synthetic beings' linked to Eden's autonomous AI artists; not yet public.

name: Bitcoin Ordinals recursive inscriptions
why: Look for artist-authored recursive-inscription projects where holders' inscriptions compose a shared work.

name: Kacie Kinzer — Tweenbots (2009)
why: Small robot of the late 2000s that, like hitchBOT, could only reach its destination if strangers helped it; named on hitchBOT's Wikipedia page as a similar project. Confirm creator, year and media.

name: Rafael Lozano-Hemmer — Voz Alta (2008)
why: Public-voice work for the memorial of the 1968 Tlatelolco massacre in Mexico City, reportedly turning what anyone says into a megaphone into searchlight flashes; confirm details and media on lozano-hemmer.com.

name: Songcamp — Camp Elektra (2021)
why: Second Songcamp camp; three songs released as 1-of-1 NFTs whose value split proved hard to divide, which led to the Chaos design; check its own release rules.

name: Blast Theory — Uncle Roy All Around You (2003) and other games
why: Further Blast Theory games mixing online and street players; check which ones give the public a rule-bound role beyond a single player.

name: eBoy, TOWR (fxhash open-form, 2025)
why: Open-form pixel towers where each collector evolution stacks new blocks (one collector stacked 37); a second open-form work worth an entry, but fxhash closed in August 2026, so media must come from elsewhere.

name: Billy Rennekamp, Clovers Network (2018)
why: Rennekamp's Ethereum project around registering rare Reversi game boards ('clovers'); check rules, authorship and media.

name: JODI & Billy Rennekamp, Chameleon (2021)
why: Folia work credited to Joan Heemskerk (JODI) and Billy Rennekamp in its source code; mechanics not yet checked.

name: Sarah Friend, Remembering Network (2019)
why: Peer-to-peer 'seed vault' memorial to threatened species on IPFS, described as open to contributions (shown at IPFS Camp and Radical Networks, 2019); check how contributors add to it before adding.

name: Sarah Friend, Portal Constellation: Reviving the Webring (2020)
why: Functional webring made in an Arebyte On Screen residency and installed on other artists' sites; check whether members' linking is framed as the work.

name: Snark.art, other artist projects (2018–)
why: The studio lists about a dozen further blockchain projects on snark.art after 89 Seconds Atomized; check which give owners a shared rule.

name: Coin Artist, The Dark Wallet Puzzle (2014)
why: Her first crypto-puzzle, a set of 12 puzzles for the Bitcoin community whose complexity was meant to make people work together (Bitcoin Magazine, July 2014); find primary documentation and images before adding.

name: Yvonne Rainer: Passing and Jostling While Confined to a Small Apartment (2020)
why: Rainer adapted Terrain (1963) into written rules and photographs in the New York Times for readers to perform at home during the COVID-19 lockdown; find the article and an image.

name: Walter De Maria: Boxes for Meaningless Work (1961)
why: Boxes with an instruction to move things from one to the other while knowing the act is meaningless; check whether viewers carry it out and find an image.

name: Earle Brown: Twenty-Five Pages (1953) and Available Forms I (1961)
why: Open-form scores in which one to twenty-five pianists, or a conductor in performance, choose the order of the pages.

name: Olafur Eliasson: Green light — An artistic workshop
why: Workshop in which refugees, migrants and visitors assemble lamps together; check whether the rules make the group's work the artwork.

name: Clemente Padín, Festival de la Postal Creativa (Galería U, Montevideo, 1974)
why: Described as the first documented mail-art exhibition in Latin America; check whether its open call set the no-jury, show-everything rules of mail-art shows.

name: Feral File and MoMA, MoMA Postcard (2023–2024)
why: Online project in which each postcard has 15 blank stamps; participants design a pixel stamp, record it on chain and pass the card on. Check authorship and media.

name: Hans Haacke, World Poll (Venice Biennale, 2015)
why: Visitors answer a questionnaire on iPads and the tallies are shown; sibling of MoMA Poll. Needs a description source.

name: Hans Haacke, John Weber Gallery Visitors' Profile (1972–73)
why: Visitors fill in a 20-question survey; results shown as charts in the gallery. Needs media.

name: Lee Mingwei, Sonic Blossom (2013), The Letter Writing Project (1998) and The Dining Project (1997)
why: Singers offer a stranger the gift of a Schubert song; visitors write letters they never sent and the museum posts them; a host shares a meal with a visitor. Need verifiable media (leemingwei.com is gone).

name: terra0, courtyard project in Strange Rules (Venice, 2026)
why: Strange Rules shows a terra0 project in the Palazzo Diedo courtyard; identify the work and add it to the strange-rules collection.

name: Agnieszka Kurant, work in Strange Rules (Venice, 2026)
why: Kurant's works use collective intelligence (crowds, termites, social-media sentiment); identify the Strange Rules work and test it.

name: Stephen Willats, Social Resource Project for Tennis Clubs (Nottingham, 1971–72)
why: Members of four tennis clubs were to remodel the game around their reasons for joining; the project was not completed. Check whether it belongs as a work.

name: World Computer Sculpture Garden contracts: Echoes (0xhaiku), Dear God, Layer of Roads (Travelers) (Figure31), Yesbot (Sarah Friend), Critique of This Show (Rhea Myers et al.), Real Abstraction (Paul Seidler)
why: Participatory contracts in the 2024 contract show (visitors add words, move travellers, toggle Is Art, post critiques, draw walls); their sites are script-only pages without images, so they were not added. Look for images or videos on the artists' own channels.

name: Casey Rodarmor, Ordinals protocol (2023)
why: Droitcour argues the protocol is an artwork made by an artist for other artists and kept alive by collective inscription; check against the inclusion test under onchain (substrate bitcoin).

name: Peter Bauman, 'The Cerebral Samba: Protocol Art, Worldbuilding & Our Two Brains' (Le Random, 2026)
why: Second Le Random essay on protocol art and worldbuilding (11 May 2026); check whether it adds to living-aesthetics.

name: Kate Sloan, Behaviourist Art and Cybernetics: Mapping a Field (Routledge, 2025)
why: Book that takes Ascott's 1966–67 essay as the starting point for a history of behaviourist art, 1945–1975 (DOI 10.4324/9781032615301).

name: Simon Denny, Proof of Work (Schinkel Pavillon, Berlin)
why: Exhibition that included Distributed Gallery's Chaos Machine; check whether it gathers enough protocol works to be a collection.

name: Botto, p5.botto (2024–2025)
why: Botto's study of p5.js code art: weekly rounds from March 2024 where anyone could vote without staking (one equal vote per sketch), then self-evolution and a community pruning of 5,000+ sketches to 22 on-chain algorithms auctioned with Verse ('Algorithmic Evolution', London, February 2025). In scope but first public in 2024.

name: Operator, Repeat as necessary: Performance Operating System (2025)
why: Ania Catherine and Dejha Ti's on-chain system holding choreography, notation, music and a conservation manual so anyone can restage a 31-minute ritual performance (premiere Scorpios Bodrum, 9–10 August 2025); 40 on-chain SVG works whose state shifts when one wallet holds a token from each chapter. Prix Ars Electronica 2026 Honorary Mention. Score/onchain scope rather than autonomous. Video: https://vimeo.com/1171859071

name: Parag K. Mital, The Game of Whispers (2026)
why: Multiplayer game in which each character is run by an AI agent that pursues goals by spreading misinformation (Prix Ars Electronica 2026 Honorary Mention); check whether human players act under authored rules.

name: Primavera De Filippi, Will Papper, Adrien Guerrera & Jake Hartnell, Aminals (GLITCH)
why: Fully on-chain lifeforms that feed on cryptocurrency and evolve as new SVG genes are added to their code; listed by the GLITCH collective. Launch date and who may add genes not verified; aminals.xyz is now a parked domain.

name: dmstfctn, Fango 1000 (2024–25)
why: On-chain 'large lore model' game built with MUD: players join Monks, Scholars or Fools, write interpretations of 1,000 chronicles and vote by throwing mud, so only consensus texts survive. Prototypes shown in 2024 (Koelhuis Eindhoven, Etopia Zaragoza), free-to-play testnet release 2025; outside this batch's 2025+ window by first showing.

name: 0xfff, Transaction Sculptures (2018–2026)
why: Arrangements of Ethereum contracts that pass value between each other; anyone can send ETH through a sculpture and the path is drawn. Shown in 1 BILLION DOLLAR SHOW, Nguyen Wahed, New York (25 Sep–19 Oct 2026). Needs per-sculpture rules and first-deployment dates.

name: DX Research Group, DX Terminal (2025) and DX Terminal Pro (2026)
why: Simulation in which about 36,000 AI trader personas act on players' instructions with trading data published on-chain (pixel art by Gremplin). Check whether it is an authored art protocol or a commercial game.

name: CROSSLUCID, The Way of Flowers (2023–2025)
why: Blockchain-registered digital seeds change form when collectors fund verified conservation projects (Regen Network, ArtEcology); solo show at Office Impart, Berlin, 2025. First iteration 2023; needs chain and contract details.

name: Figure31, DEAD ENDS (Canto, 2022)
why: Each mint comes with $UP tokens that collectors spend to upsample images up to five times, shaping the final collection together.

name: Figure31, Reaper's Gambit (2023)
why: $RG becomes non-transferable after 64,800 blocks unless holders move it to a new address; holders can burn it into an 'Immortal' NFT.

name: Figure31, LINE (Fingerprints DAO, 2024)
why: 100 dynamic NFTs whose holders move them to new grid coordinates; position decides the image each token sees.

name: Matt Kane, ANONS & Multitudes (2023–)
why: Auction-based series by an existing gallery artist; rules not yet checked.

name: Leander Herzog, 1000 True Fans (2023)
why: Title suggests a patronage protocol; not yet checked.

name: Anna Ridler, The Shell Record: Breathings of the Moon
why: Machine-made shell images that can be seen and traded only at low tide on the Thames; check year and whether the tide rule shapes collector behaviour.

name: Ana María Caballero, In Record Time (2025)
why: OpenSea and Art Basel commission for Zero 10: an open edition built around the poem Training Data, which Caballero invited other artists to annotate by hand (continuing her Fifty Ways of Looking at a Poem). Check whether the annotators' contributions are recorded on-chain and how many took part.

name: Ed Fornieles & Nina Runa Essendrop, Cel (2019)
why: Larp simulation of an extremist online community, shown in Worldglimpsing (ArkDes 2025–26); add to that collection if researched.

name: Rimini Protokoll: Call Cutta in a Box (2008), 100% City (2008–), Remote X (2013), Situation Rooms (2013)
why: Earlier works where audiences follow headphone, phone or tablet instructions and become the performers.

name: OMSK Social Club: Cryptorave, Perception as Participation, Worlds' End Hackathon (2024) and other Real Game Play works
why: Earlier role-play frameworks for crowds; only the 2025–26 works are in this batch.

name: Christian Falsnaes, audience-instruction performances (JEG/I/MOI 2024; Randers performance collaboration 2025)
why: Danish artist whose performances consist of instructions the audience carries out; no 2025–26 work found with enough documentation.

name: Operator (Ania Catherine & Dejha Ti), Repeat as necessary: Performance Operating System (2025–26)
why: 31-minute ritual guiding audience-participants, with choreography, score and music stored on-chain so anyone can restage it; Prix Ars Electronica 2026 Honorary Mention. Belongs to an on-chain pass.

name: Júlia Nueno Guitart, Sabot – Riding the Algorithm (2022–)
why: Open-source app built with delivery riders that pools their data into a rider-governed commons; Prix Ars Electronica 2026 Honorary Mention. Prototype dates from 2022, outside this batch's dates.

name: Draw a Fish (drawafish.com, 2025)
why: Viral shared fish tank: drawings must pass an AI 'is it a fish' check, then swim with everyone's fish and are voted on. Creator and launch date not yet verified from a reliable source.

name: Benediktas Gylys, The Portal (Vilnius–Lublin 2021; Dublin–New York 2024)
why: Telematic public sculptures linking two cities by silent live video; paused in May 2024 after misuse, later moved to Philadelphia.

name: Elliott Cost, One Minute Park (Tiny Awards 2024 winner)
why: Plays 60-second videos of parks filmed and submitted by volunteers around the world; crowdsourced. Launch year to verify; add to tiny-awards if researched.

name: Tiny Awards 2024 Multiplayer finalists: Cursorwatching, Internet Fridge, Internet Stoop, Stranger Video, 7 Minutes in Heaven
why: Small multiplayer websites shortlisted next to One Million Checkboxes; check which have a clear collective rule (Internet Fridge is by Spencer Chang, Stranger Video by Nolen Royalty).

name: Scores for Meeting Otherwise, ed. Aio Frei, Franziska Koch and Irene Revell (Silver Press, November 2026)
why: Feminist history of the performance score from Pauline Oliveros onward, with newly commissioned scores; not yet published on 17 October 2026.

name: Lauren Lee McCarthy, HOST (party performance with AI earpiece directions)
why: Guests receive private directions from an AI through earpieces and choose whether to follow them; commissioned by The Music Center, Los Angeles. Date not stated on the artist's site.

name: Tino Sehgal, new lobby work at Leeum Museum of Art (Seoul, 2026)
why: New constructed situation shown in his first Korean solo show (March–June 2026); no description beyond press notes.

name: Improv Everywhere, The Mp3 Experiment (2004–; 21st edition 2025)
why: Annual mass event: participants download one audio file, press play at the same moment and follow its synchronized instructions in public; only Frozen Grand Central is in the gallery so far.

name: Mehtap Baydu, Analı Kızlı – With Mothers and Daughters (Manifesta 16 Ruhr, 2026)
why: A collective of 12 women from Bochum cooks a meal for guests who would not normally meet, in a former church; check the seating and invitation rules.
